result: The manuscript provides background on Gaucher disease (GD), its classification, molecular basis, clinical manifestations, current treatments, and the role of microglia in neurodegeneration.
evaluation: Claims C1-C16 establish well-documented background knowledge about GD, supported by multiple citations to established literature. These claims provide context for the study but do not represent novel findings from the current work.

result: In nGD mice (Gbalsl/lsl), there is progressive infiltration of CCR2+ macrophages, attrition of homeostatic microglia, and accumulation of diverse immune cells coinciding with neurodegeneration. Microglia and immune infiltrates accumulate GluCer and GlcSph and exhibit upregulation of type 1 interferon signature genes and disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes.
evaluation: Claims C17-C24 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 1A-B), scRNA-seq analysis (Figure 1C-D), lipidomics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and total RNA-seq (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C). The temporal analysis and multi-modal data provide strong evidence for the immune landscape changes in nGD.

result: Restoration of Gba in microglia (nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+) increased survival more than twofold, while restoration in neurons (nGD NesCre/+) extended survival to ~200 days. Both interventions reduced brain GluCer/GlcSph levels (50-98% reduction) and altered immune cell profiles, with neuronal rescue showing more complete normalization of microglia and immune infiltration.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by survival data (Figure 2B), flow cytometry (Figure 2C-F), and comprehensive lipidomics (Figure 2G). The differential effects of microglia vs. neuronal rescue are well-documented with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

result: Microglia-specific deletion of Gba (Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+) results in accumulation of GlcSph and GluCer species in the brain, with young mice appearing healthy but aged mice (~12 months) developing motor deficits, elevated serum GlcSph, microglial attrition, and increased CCR2+ macrophage infiltration. scRNA-seq revealed age-dependent transition from homeostatic to DAM phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are supported by lipidomics (Figure 3A-B), flow cytometry (Figure 3C), and scRNA-seq data (Figure 3D-G). The age-dependent progression provides a model for late-onset neurodegeneration. However, C32 notes behavioral data are not shown, which is a minor limitation.

result: nGD mouse models exhibit prominent infiltration of GzmA+ NK cells in the brain, with higher percentages in nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice compared to nGD mice. NK cell activation appears brain-specific as splenic NK cells were unaltered. This phenotype was replicated in a chemically-induced nGD model using CBE.
evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4A-L) across multiple models. The brain-specific NK cell activation (C40) and replication in CBE model (C42-C44) strengthen the findings. C41 shows no S1P accumulation, suggesting alternative mechanisms for NK recruitment.

result: Single-nucleus RNA-seq revealed that lysosomal biology, ISG, and ApoE genes were highly upregulated in multiple brain cell types (microglia, neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes) in nGD and 6-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice, but not in 2-week-old nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice. Neuronal Gba rescue normalized these pathways. Disease-associated astrocyte (DAA) genes were induced in nGD and 6-week nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
evaluation: Claims C45-C53 are supported by comprehensive snRNA-seq analysis (Figure 5A-F) with appropriate clustering, pathway analysis, and temporal comparisons. The data demonstrate cell-type-specific and time-dependent effects of Gba deficiency and rescue. The large number of DEGs (C49) and pathway enrichment analyses provide robust support.

result: Astrocytes and activated microglia from nGD mice showed elevated ROS levels (measured by CellROX) and increased accumulation of neutral lipids (measured by BODIPY staining) compared to controls.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 5G-J). These findings complement the transcriptional data showing oxidative stress pathways. The use of established fluorescent probes provides direct functional evidence.

result: Treatment with GCS inhibitor GZ-161 significantly prolonged survival in nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice, normalized serum GlcSph levels, reduced CCR2+ macrophages, restored homeostatic microglia, and reduced Pro-IL-1β+ microglia and GzmA+ immune cells. GZ-161 also reduced NK cell infiltration in the CBE model.
evaluation: Claims C57-C62 are supported by survival data (Figure 6A), lipidomics (Figure 6B), and flow cytometry (Figure 6C-H). The therapeutic effects are demonstrated across multiple models. However, C60 notes GZ-161 had no effect on immune infiltrates in nGD mice, suggesting model-dependent efficacy.

result: In aged Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice, GZ-161 treatment normalized HexCer accumulation in corpus callosum and cerebral cortex (measured by MALDI imaging), reduced DAM cluster 2 while enhancing homeostatic microglia clusters (by scRNA-seq), and reduced expression of Gzma, Ccl5, Tyrobp, and Klf2 in NK cells.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by MALDI imaging (Figure 7A) and scRNA-seq data (Figure 7D-E). The spatial resolution of lipid changes and single-cell transcriptional changes provide strong mechanistic evidence for GZ-161 effects in the late-onset model.

result: Serum Nf-L levels were massively elevated in nGD mice (2000-fold), moderately elevated in nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ (~100-fold), and mildly elevated in nGD NesCre/+ (~20-fold) compared to controls. GZ-161 treatment significantly reduced serum Nf-L in both nGD and nGD Cx3cr1Cre/+ mice. Serum Nf-L strongly correlated with serum GlcSph (r=0.8344, p<0.0001) and increased with age in Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice.
evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by Simoa measurements (Figure 8A-C) with appropriate sample sizes and statistical analysis. The strong correlation between Nf-L and GlcSph (C72) provides compelling evidence linking lipid accumulation to neurodegeneration. The dose-response relationship across genotypes strengthens the findings.

result: In human GD patients, serum Nf-L levels were elevated in GD3 patients compared to age-matched GD1 patients, associated with elevated serum GlcSph. Adult GD1 patients had significantly higher serum Nf-L than children with GD1 and adult healthy controls.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75 are supported by patient sample analysis (Figure 8D-F). The translation from mouse models to human patients strengthens the biomarker candidacy of Nf-L. However, the patient cohort sizes are relatively small (n=5 GD3, n=6 age-matched GD1 for C73-C74), which limits generalizability.

result: LysoPC showed strong accumulation in microglia of cerebral cortex and midbrain in untreated Gbafl/flCx3cr1Cre/+ mice, which was significantly reduced by GZ-161 treatment. Older GD1 patients exhibited increased serum LysoPC 16:1 compared to young GD1 patients.
evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by MALDI imaging (Figure 8G) and patient serum analysis (Figure 8H). The identification of LysoPC as a co-regulated lipid provides new mechanistic insights. Translation to human patients supports its potential as a biomarker.

result: ApoE expression was prominently induced in astrocytes, activated microglia, multiple neuronal cell types, and endothelial cells in nGD mice, with concomitant induction of Abca1. Sera of untreated GD1 patients showed markedly increased ApoE levels compared to healthy controls, which decreased after ERT. Elevated ApoE correlated with serum GlcSph (p<0.001) with ROC AUC of 0.92 (p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C79-C85 are supported by snRNA-seq data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B), patient serum measurements (Figure 8I-K), and ROC analysis (Figure 8L). The strong correlation with GlcSph, response to ERT, and high ROC AUC support ApoE as a robust biomarker. The multi-cell-type expression pattern provides mechanistic context.

result: Summary claims from the abstract stating that targeted Gba rescue in microglia and neurons reversed GluCer/GlcSph buildup, ameliorated neuroinflammation, reduced serum Nf-L, and improved survival. Serum GlcSph correlated with Nf-L and ApoE in both mouse models and GD patients. GCS inhibitor treatment enhanced survival and reversed neuroinflammation involving microglia, NK cells, astrocytes, and neurons.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are high-level summary statements supported by the collective evidence from multiple figures throughout the manuscript. These integrate findings from genetic rescue experiments, pharmacological intervention, and biomarker validation.

result: The study cohort consisted of 51 type 1 GD patients with at least one N370S mutation (mean age 63.9 years), 5 GD type 3 patients (homozygous L444P), and 28 healthy controls (mean age 38 years).
evaluation: Claims C90-C92 describe the patient cohort used in the study. These are straightforward demographic descriptions that are adequately documented in the Methods section and Figure 9.

result: Background information on nGD mouse phenotype and microglial biology from prior literature.
evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by citations to prior work (Enquist et al., 2007; Dick et al., 2022) and represent established knowledge used to contextualize the current findings.
